title: region-traffic-steering-and-leadership-patterns-brain-dump
body:
TL;DR: this is a living brain-dump contrasting three practical multiregion control-plane topologies and concrete tradeoffs for routing and leader election. Goal: pick a pattern we can implement in Q1 as an MLP (minimum lovable product) for Dedicated + Private customers with clear DR runbook and measurable SLOs.

Background/context
- Problem: keep control-plane operations (routing decisions, policy enforcement, rollout orchestration) available and predictable across regions while minimizing cross-region write-latency and blast radius.
- Constraints: some tenants will be geo-bound (data residency), others need global consistency for rollouts, and we must support quick failover for Dedicated customers with SLA expectations.
- Assumption: data plane (inference) is region-local. Control plane is what we're designing.

Candidate topologies (short names):
1) Split-ownership active-active (per-tenant regional primary)
   - Each tenant has a single region designated as their control-plane leader (owned by tenant metadata). Global API endpoints route to the tenant's leader for writes, with read-only mirrors in other regions.
   - Leader election is explicit (metadata flag + lease). Failover: another region picks up the leader and migrates the ownership flag.
   - Pros: minimizes cross-region control writes, simpler state model for each tenant; fast per-tenant failover; clear boundary for data residency.
   - Cons: requires robust routing to the tenant primary; if leader region goes down, per-tenant failover may cause warmup/latency spikes.

2) Global active-active (stateless controllers + global consensus for critical ops)
   - Each region runs stateless control-plane instances that can accept requests for any tenant. Critical metadata stored in a strongly-consistent global store (e.g., managed Riak/Consul/etcd with multi-region replication) or via per-resource quorum arbitration (more on the latter).
   - Leader election is lightweight or per-operation (optimistic concurrency, compare-and-swap for write ops).
   - Pros: zero routing surprises, uniform latency for control-plane requests; natural scale and high availability.
   - Cons: complexity in achieving truly low-latency writes (global consensus will increase tail latency), cost of replication, and harder to meet strict data residency without additional config.

3) Active-passive regional fabric (cold standby with fast promotion)
   - One region is active for all tenants by default; others are passive but maintain warmed state asynchronously. In failure, passive is promoted via a coordinated orchestration runbook.
   - Leader election is explicit and centralized (global arbiter or runbook-driven).
   - Pros: simple leadership semantics, usually cheapest (fewer cross-region consensus requirements).
   - Cons: failover can be disruptive unless we invest heavily in warming/priming passive regions.

Leader election approaches (tradeoffs)
- Lease-based via distributed KV (etcd-style TTL leases): good when you want short, deterministic leader terms. Needs reliable clocks and lease renewal -> can be brittle under network partitions.
- Raft cluster spanning regions: strong safety, but cross-region latency makes elections and log replication expensive. Better if we partition Raft per-tenant or per-shard to reduce global consensus footprint.
- Hybrid: local Raft per-region for fast local leadership + global arbiter (small quorum) for cross-region leader handoff. Global arbiter only used for border cases.
- Soft leader (optimistic ownership): accept writes anywhere, use CRDT-style merges or last-writer-wins for non-critical metadata. This reduces latency but complicates correctness and audits.

Routing & traffic steering
- Client-side SDKs (preferred for latency-sensitive requests): SDK selects region based on routing table returned at init; SDK supports sticky routing and automatic fallback. Pros: low lat, fewer hops. Cons: SDK rollout complexity and caching TTL management.
- Edge routers (global LB + edge proxies): route requests to appropriate control-plane region via geo policies + capacity signals. Easier to change routing centrally.
- DNS-based geo-routing: cheap but slow to change (TTL) and poor for quick failover.
- Anycast + intelligent routers: fast failover but suffers from opaque routing decisions (BGP level).
- Policy examples: region-preferred -> prefer tenant primary; capacity-aware -> divert to cheaper/less-busy region for non-critical ops; latency-SLO-first -> prioritize nearest region even if not tenant primary for reads.

State placement and consistency
- Categorize control state by consistency needs: a) critical authoritative config (rollout pins, billing tiers) => strong consistency; b) transient telemetry and cache metadata => eventual fine; c) KV cache for inference prefix -> local only with async replication.
- Approach: keep authoritative config in a small strongly-consistent store (per-tenant keys sharded) and replicate read-only caches closer to serving regions. For writes, route to the shard owner (see split-ownership).

DR runbook (sketch)
- Detection: health checks + leader-heartbeat monitor + SLO alarm triggers.
- Automated escalation: if region X leader heartbeat fails X times in Y secs, mark degraded and begin traffic diversion.
- Pre-failover steps: mark primary read-only if possible (drain in-flight ops), publish new routing table to edge and SDK channel, begin DNS change only as fallback.
- Promotion: pick next region (preference order per-tenant), acquire lease, replay last known authoritative metadata, warm caches (KV/agent sync), start accepting writes.
- Verification: smoke test API, check rollout state machine, fire synthetic inference requests through promoted control plane to ensure flow-through to region-local data plane.
- Rollback: if failures exceed thresholds, revert routing and de-promote; capture a post-mortem trigger.

Observability & SLOs to track
- Leader change rate (changes/hour) — aim: < 1/week for stable tenants.
- Failover time (detection -> promotion) — target: < 60s automated, < 5min manual.
- Control-plane P99 tail latency by operation type (reads vs writes).
- Cross-region control write latency percentiles (critical for active-active).
- Error rate correlated with region outages and leader transitions.
- Traffic diverted % and cost delta during failovers.

Testing strategy
- Chaos tests: inject asymmetric latency and packet loss between regions, simulate leader flaps, test lease expiry handling.
- DR drills: quarterly table-top + annual live cutover for a small customer subset.
- Synthetic load tests that exercise global consensus under scale (simulate many concurrent tenant writes).

Cost & ops considerations
- Active-active with strong consistency increases egress and replication costs significantly; quantify by model tenant and multiply by region count.
- Active-passive cheaper but ops heavy (human-in-the-loop may be required initially).
- Split-ownership can be mixed: some tenants (enterprise) get single-region primaries; PLG tenants default to multi-region active-active with weaker guarantees.

Open questions / unresolved engineering decisions
- Do we want to charge a price delta for single-region vs global control-plane SLA? (billing + product)
- Global arbiter: implement as small Quorum-as-a-Service? Who runs it in Private deployments?
- How to handle long-lived leases when customers do controlled region moves? (migration primitives)
- Rollout of SDK-based routing vs server-side steering — which to prioritize in Q1 for the smallest operational burden?

Immediate next steps (action items)
- [ ] Prototype split-ownership flow: tenant metadata shard -> route table -> SDK fallback. Owner: Maya. Jira: PLAT-987.
- [ ] Run simulated failover test against ephemeral infra (k8s clusters across three zones) and measure failover time. Owner: Liam. PR: control-plane#342.
- [ ] Draft public runbook (customer-facing) for Dedicated customers describing failover expectations and how to request manual relocation. Owner: Ethan.

Notes-to-self / random thoughts
- Consider tagging tenants with a "failover-policy" enum: immediate-auto-promote | manual-approve | never-migrate. Makes runbook deterministic.
- For private/on-prem installs, assume no cross-region consensus: split-ownership or active-passive only. Document constraints.
- We should log every leadership transition with causal trace id so we can replay decisions during postmortems.

References & pointers
- See ticket PLAT-987 (routing prototype) and PR control-plane#342 for early leader-election code.
- Confluence page for SLOs (linked above).

End of brain-dump. This is intentionally rough — aim is to converge on one recommended pattern next week and start a small spike to validate failover timings and cost profile.

Unresolved: whether to prioritize SDK routing (lower latency) vs central router (simpler ops) for Q1 MLP. Will discuss in sync with product next Wed.
